questions.question: When Socrates says that the true philosopher 'practices for dying and death,' he means:
options: A. Philosophers should study death and burial customs
B. Philosophy is depressing and preoccupied with morbid topics
C. The philosophical life is a gradual purification of the soul from bodily distraction — a practice of separation that death completes
D. Philosophers accept that their views will be forgotten after death and write accordingly
questions.explanation: Plato's argument is that philosophy frees the soul from attachment to the body's misleading desires and imprecise sensory information, orienting it toward the eternal Forms. Death — the complete separation of soul from body — is the culmination of this process. The philosopher has been practicing this separation throughout life; death is not a loss but a completion.

questions.question: Briefly state the Affinity Argument for the soul's immortality. What is its main strength and its main weakness?
questions.sample_answer: The Affinity Argument: the soul resembles the eternal, invisible, unchanging realm of Forms, while the body resembles the visible, composite, changeable realm. When a purified soul departs the body, it will naturally gravitate toward what it is akin to — the divine, intelligible realm. Strength: it connects the soul's nature directly to the Theory of Forms, integrating the metaphysics and the immortality argument. Weakness: the argument only establishes likelihood, not certainty — Socrates acknowledges this. It also assumes the soul has genuine kinship with the Forms, which is not independently proven within this argument.

questions.question: The Final Argument (the Life-Form argument) claims that the soul cannot admit death because it participates essentially in the Form of Life.
questions.explanation: The Final Argument works by analogy: fire cannot admit coldness while remaining fire; snow cannot admit heat while remaining snow. The soul cannot admit death (the Form of Death) while remaining a soul, because the soul always brings life with it essentially — it participates in the Form of Life. Therefore, when confronted with death, the soul must either withdraw (survive) or cease to be a soul. Plato argues that its indestructible nature means it withdraws.

questions.question: How does the Phaedo connect to the Argument from Recollection in the Meno?
options: A. The Phaedo contradicts the Meno by claiming the soul does not have pre-natal knowledge
B. The Phaedo uses recollection as evidence that the soul existed before birth — and from this argues for post-mortem survival
C. The Phaedo ignores the Meno and starts the recollection argument from scratch
D. The Phaedo's second argument shows that recollection is impossible
questions.explanation: The Argument from Recollection in the Phaedo builds directly on the Meno: since we recognize the Form of Equality (for example) when we see imperfect physical instances of it, we must have known perfect Equality before birth. This establishes pre-natal existence of the soul. From pre-natal existence, Plato argues there is reason to think the soul may also survive death — the soul was not born when the body was born, so it may not die when the body dies.

questions.question: Aristotle would reject the soul-body dualism in the Phaedo. What would he say instead about the relationship between soul and body?
questions.sample_answer: Aristotle holds that the soul is the form of the body — it is the organizing principle that makes a living body actually alive and capable of its functions, not a separable entity that exists independently of the body. For Aristotle, asking whether the soul can survive without the body is like asking whether the shape of a wax seal can exist without the wax. When the body dies, the soul does not migrate to another realm; it simply ceases to be, as the wax loses its shape when melted. This is why Aristotle's ethics focuses entirely on the good life in this world — not on preparation for another.
